traveler: Louis XIV, roi de France et de Navarre, called Louis le Grand and le Roi-Soleil
title: The God-Given: Saint-Germain to Versailles, and the Trench at Saint-Denis
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The God-Given Child and the Barricades

stops.name: Saint-Germain-en-Laye: the birth of the Dieudonne
stops.date_confidence: attested. The research pool gave 48.8947, 2.0947, about 390 m off; corrected here to Wikipedia's 48.89806, 2.09639. A second correction cannot be applied at all: he was born in the Chateau Neuf, demolished after the Revolution, and every modern coordinate for the site points at the surviving Chateau Vieux beside it.
stops.campa: Twenty-three years into a marriage that has produced no living heir, Anne of Austria is delivered of a son on the terrace above the Seine at Saint-Germain-en-Laye. France has been praying for this birth on royal order. They name him Louis Dieudonne, the God-given, and the word is meant literally: a kingdom that had begun preparing for a disputed succession is handed a boy instead. His father has five years left. The building he is born in, the Chateau Neuf, will be pulled down after the Revolution, and the pin now falls on the old castle next door.
suggested_refs: The site of the demolished Chateau Neuf at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, birthplace of Louis XIV

stops.name: Saint-Germain-en-Laye: a king at four
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Louis XIII dies in the same chateau where his son was born, and a boy of four years and eight months becomes king of France. Four days later Anne of Austria goes to the Parlement of Paris, has her husband's will annulled and the council it created dissolved, and is made sole regent. She keeps the man the will had saddled her with: Cardinal Mazarin, an Italian the court detests and cannot do without. For eighteen years France is governed by a foreigner in the name of a child who watches and says nothing.
stops.quote: Nature was responsible for the first knots which tied me to my mother. But attachments formed later by shared qualities of the spirit are far more difficult to break than those formed merely by blood.
stops.quote_source: Louis XIV, English translation as printed in the Wikipedia article 'Louis XIV', footnote 9; seen on the live article and not traced by this pool to a primary edition
suggested_refs: The Parlement of Paris act of 18 May 1643 annulling the will of Louis XIII

stops.name: Paris: the Day of the Barricades
stops.date_confidence: attested, 26 to 28 August 1648. The research pool dated the opening of the Fronde to 22 October 1648, which verification rejected outright: nothing attaches to that date, and the misreading probably comes from the Fronde chronology's 24 October 1648 entry for the Peace of Westphalia.
stops.campa: Mazarin arrests the leaders of the Parlement of Paris, and the city answers overnight. Barricades go up in the streets between the Palais-Royal and the Ile de la Cite, chains across the bridges, armed men at every crossing, and the government gives its prisoners back within two days. Louis is nine years old and inside the palace the barricades enclose. He will say for the rest of his life that a king can be besieged in Paris, in his own capital, by his own subjects.
suggested_refs: The Fronde barricades of 26 to 28 August 1648 in the streets of central Paris

stops.name: Palais-Royal, Paris: the flight by night
stops.date_confidence: attested, the night of 5 to 6 January 1649
stops.campa: On the night of Epiphany the regent has the household woken without lights and taken out of the Palais-Royal in carriages, out of Paris, to Saint-Germain. The court arrives at a chateau stripped of its furniture; the king of France sleeps on straw while Conde blockades his capital. In March the Peace of Rueil ends this first Fronde with almost no blood spilled and settles nothing. Louis is ten. Thirty-three years later he will move the government of France twelve miles out of Paris and never once explain why.
suggested_refs: The Peace of Rueil, 11 March 1649, ending the Fronde of the parlement
sources: Bluche and Voltaire's Siecle de Louis XIV are cited by the research pool for the straw at Saint-Germain but were not fetched; that detail is reported, not verified

stops.name: Paris: the king comes back and the Fronde ends
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Four years of aristocratic revolt have used up the appetite for it. After Conde's army is mauled at the Faubourg Saint-Antoine and the city turns against the princes, Paris sends for its king. Louis re-enters to acclamation, fourteen months past the majority declared for him at thirteen. In February Mazarin rides back unopposed, and the Fronde is finished. Louis governs nothing yet. The nobility has kept its own armies and turned them on him twice; he spends the next fifty years taking those armies away.
suggested_refs: The Battle of the Faubourg Saint-Antoine, 2 July 1652, and the burning of the Hotel de Ville

stops.name: Reims: anointed with the oil of Clovis
stops.date_confidence: attested. Pin inherited from louis_xvi.journey.json, which uses 49.2533, 4.0347; the interlock lens reported 49.2528, 4.0347, which is not the value in that file.
stops.campa: The oil comes up from Saint-Remi in the Sainte Ampoule, the phial that tradition says descended from heaven for the baptism of Clovis, and Louis is anointed with it at fifteen. He receives the sword called Charlemagne's and is crowned before the peers of France. Mazarin still governs and will for seven more years. Reims gives him no power at all. It gives him the thing French power is measured against. The same phial will be broken over Louis XVI in this church in 1775, and smashed in the street outside in 1793.
suggested_refs: The Sainte Ampoule of Reims, used at the consecration of Clovis, Louis XIV and Louis XVI
sources: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Louis XIV of France'

stops.name: Arras: the anointed boy goes to the war
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unknown and defaulted to 01. The research pool rests this stop on general military histories of the Franco-Spanish war rather than on a document; the campaign is far better attested than Louis's exact part in it.
stops.campa: Two months after Reims the king travels with the army. Spain has been besieging Arras since July; Turenne comes up in August, breaks the lines, and the Spanish leave their guns in the trenches. Louis is present, not commanding. Conde, who blockaded him in Paris five years ago, is in the field opposite him now under Spanish command. This is the frontier he will spend the next fifty years pushing north town by town, and Arras is the first fortified place he sees taken.
suggested_refs: Turenne's relief of the Spanish siege of Arras, August 1654
sources: standard military histories of the Franco-Spanish War 1635-1659, cited by the research pool without an edition

stops.name: Pheasant Island: the treaty that buys a marriage
stops.date_confidence: attested for the signing. The research pool attached Louis's first sight of his bride to this day, which verification moved: he was not present in November 1659, and the family interview on this island took place in June 1660, seven months later.
stops.campa: On a low island in the Bidasoa, neutral ground between two crowns, Mazarin and Luis de Haro sign the Treaty of the Pyrenees and end twenty-four years of war with Spain. The price and the seal is a marriage: the infanta Maria Theresa, daughter of Philip IV, for the king of France, with renunciations written in to keep the two crowns from ever coming to rest on one head. Louis is not there. He comes to this island in June of the following year, sees the woman he is to marry for the first time, and marries her within the week.
suggested_refs: The Ile des Faisans in the Bidasoa, condominium island of the Treaty of the Pyrenees

stops.name: Saint-Jean-de-Luz: the marriage and the walled door
stops.date_confidence: attested; a proxy ceremony had been performed at Fuenterrabia on 2 June, which has no coordinate in the research pool and is carried here in the campa
stops.campa: In the church of Saint-Jean-Baptiste, a week after a proxy ceremony at Fuenterrabia across the river, Louis marries his first cousin twice over. Maria Theresa speaks no French. The door they pass through on the way out is bricked up behind them, and the town keeps it walled, on the ground that no lesser marriage should ever use it. The renunciation she signs is conditional on a dowry Spain has no means of paying, and on the strength of that unpaid sum her husband will claim the Spanish Netherlands within seven years.
suggested_refs: The walled-up door of the Church of Saint-Jean-Baptiste at Saint-Jean-de-Luz

stops.name: Notre-Dame de Paris: the entry of the king and the Spanish queen
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The king and his Spanish queen enter Paris in triumph and process to Notre-Dame for the Te Deum. The route is hung with tapestries and arches, and the corporations of the city turn out in order of precedence to see a peace made flesh in a marriage. Nothing in the day is spontaneous. The route is set weeks in advance and the city is told what to hang from it, and the reign never afterwards stops staging the king this way. Mazarin, who arranged every part of it, has seven months to live.
suggested_refs: The triumphal arches of the entree of 26 August 1660 on the Rue Saint-Antoine
sources: standard biographies cited by the research pool without an edition

stops.name: Vincennes: Mazarin dies and no one replaces him
stops.date_confidence: attested at 9 March by the geography lens; the chronology lens gives only March 1661, and the address to the ministers falls the following morning
stops.campa: Mazarin dies at Vincennes at fifty-eight, having governed France for eighteen years and assembled the largest private fortune in Europe. The next morning Louis calls the secretaries of state together and tells them there will be no first minister. He is twenty-two and has been king for eighteen years without governing a day of it. The court gives the arrangement a few weeks. He holds two councils a day for fifty-four years and dies without ever having named a successor to the cardinal.
stops.quote: Up to this moment I have been pleased to entrust the government of my affairs to the late Cardinal. It is now time that I govern them myself. You will assist me with your counsels when I ask for them. I request and order you to seal no orders except by my command ... I order you not to sign anything, not even a passport ... without my command; to render account to me personally each day and to favor no one.
stops.quote_source: Louis XIV to his secretaries of state, 10 March 1661, the day after Mazarin's death; widely reproduced English translation, given as reported rather than manuscript-verified. The research pool credited this to 'standard biographical sources' via Wikipedia footnote 31; that footnote is in fact a hobbyist website archived in 2013, and the attribution has been withdrawn here.
suggested_refs: The keep of the Chateau de Vincennes, where Mazarin died on 9 March 1661

stops.name: Vaux-le-Vicomte: the fete that cost a minister his life
stops.date_confidence: attested. The research pool's coordinate, 48.5697, 2.7136, sat about 530 m north of the chateau; corrected here to Wikipedia's 48.564851, 2.714.
stops.campa: Nicolas Fouquet, superintendent of finances, receives the king at the house Le Vau, Le Brun and Le Notre have built him. Six thousand guests are fed off gold plate. Moliere's Les Facheux is played on a stage that rises out of the garden, Vatel runs the kitchens, and the fireworks close over the canal. Louis sees in one evening exactly the machine he intends to own, working in the hands of a servant. Within three weeks Fouquet is under arrest, and within ten years those same three men are building Versailles.
suggested_refs: The gardens of Vaux-le-Vicomte as Le Notre left them for the fete of 17 August 1661

stops.name: Nantes: d'Artagnan takes the minister in the courtyard
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Fouquet leaves a council meeting in the chateau at Nantes on the king's twenty-third birthday and is taken outside by Charles de Batz-Castelmore d'Artagnan, captain of the musketeers. The trial runs three years. The court, packed and pressed, still votes banishment; Louis overrules his own tribunal and makes it imprisonment for life. Fouquet dies in the fortress of Pignerol in March 1680, nineteen years in. Colbert takes his office, his papers and his enemies, and no one man is ever again allowed to hold the money.
suggested_refs: The Chateau des ducs de Bretagne at Nantes, where Fouquet was arrested on 5 September 1661

stops.name: Fontainebleau: the Grand Dauphin
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Maria Theresa is delivered of a son at Fontainebleau, seventeen months after the wedding at Saint-Jean-de-Luz. He is Louis, called the Grand Dauphin, and he is the answer to the renunciations signed on the Bidasoa: the line is secured inside a year. Five more children follow her and not one of them lives past three. The Dauphin is tutored by Bossuet, outlives his mother by twenty-eight years, and dies of smallpox at Meudon in 1711 without having reigned a single day.
suggested_refs: The Chateau de Fontainebleau apartments where the Grand Dauphin was born

stops.name: The Louvre, Paris: Bernini sent home, Perrault built instead
stops.date_confidence: the research pool dates the Louvre residence and building campaign only to 'the 1660s'. Dated here to 1665, the year Bernini came to Paris and the year Colbert took the controller-generalship, with month and day defaulted to 01. This is an editorial choice on a vague date.
stops.campa: The court is still in Paris and the king lives in the Louvre. Colbert, made Controller-General of Finances, sends to Rome for Gian Lorenzo Bernini to design the east front. Bernini comes, is feted, produces a Roman palace that would have swallowed the old one, and goes home with a pension and no commission. Claude Perrault's colonnade is built instead, flat and cold along the whole east front. Louis keeps building in Paris for another decade and then leaves it, and the east front is finished for a king who no longer lives behind it.
suggested_refs: Perrault's colonnade on the east front of the Louvre, built after Bernini's designs were set aside

stops.name: Tournai: the town of Childeric gives up
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unknown and defaulted to 01. Pin inherited from clovis.journey.json, which places Childeric's hall at 50.6069, 3.3893; the geography lens gave the cathedral at 50.6067, 3.3888.
stops.campa: Philip IV of Spain is dead, the dowry was never paid, and Louis marches into the Spanish Netherlands claiming his wife's inheritance under a local law of devolution. Tournai capitulates almost without resistance. Fourteen years earlier, inside Louis's own minority, a mason digging in this town had broken into the grave of Childeric, father of Clovis, and lifted out three hundred golden bees; the bees are in the royal collection now, and Napoleon will have them sewn onto his coronation mantle in place of the Bourbon lily.
suggested_refs: The golden bees of Childeric, found at Tournai on 27 May 1653

stops.name: Lille: nine days, and then a citadel
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unknown and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Louis directs the siege of Lille in person and the city holds nine days. He has already bought Dunkirk from Charles II of England for five million livres and taken Douai in July; with Lille the chain of Flemish towns falls inside a single summer. Sebastien Le Prestre de Vauban is put to work ringing the city with a five-pointed citadel of brick and stone, and calls it afterwards the queen of citadels. The frontier of France stops being a line on a treaty and becomes a system of masonry.
suggested_refs: Vauban's citadel at Lille, begun 1667, the queen of citadels

stops.name: Dole: a province taken in a fortnight of snow
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unknown and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: In February, in the snow, Conde takes Dole in days and Franche-Comte in a fortnight. Spain has held the province for a century and a half. A Triple Alliance of the Dutch, the English and the Swedes forms against the speed of it, and at Aix-la-Chapelle in May Louis gives Franche-Comte back and keeps the Flemish towns. He returns in 1674 and takes the province for good, Vauban fortifies the citadel above Besancon, and the Dutch who forced the first surrender learn what it cost them.
suggested_refs: Vauban's citadel of Besancon, built after the second conquest of Franche-Comte in 1674

segments.name: Versailles Rising, and the War Against a Republic

stops.name: Chambord: Moliere plays a merchant who wants to be a gentleman
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The court comes to Chambord for the autumn hunt, and Moliere's troupe plays Le Bourgeois Gentilhomme for the king in a room of Francois I's abandoned palace, with Lully's Turkish ceremony at the end of it. The joke is a merchant buying his way into rank. The audience is a court in which every man's precedence, seat, and right to hand the king his shirt is being written down and made absolute. Nobody in the room finds the subject academic. Chambord empties again when the court leaves.
suggested_refs: The Chateau de Chambord, kept for royal visits and empty between them

stops.name: Versailles: the enveloppe closes over his father's lodge
stops.date_confidence: the research pool gives the year 1671 for the completion of Le Vau's enveloppe; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Louis Le Vau finishes the enveloppe: the small brick hunting lodge of Louis XIII is now wrapped on three sides in an Italian facade of stone, terraced toward the gardens, with the old court surviving inside it like a stone in fruit. Le Notre is moving water and earth on a scale that takes a regiment to do it, and the marsh below the terrace is being dug into a canal. Louis refuses to demolish his father's building, and he will refuse every architect who proposes it for the next forty years.
suggested_refs: The brick and stone court of Louis XIII surviving at the heart of Versailles

stops.name: Chantilly: Vatel and the fish that came late
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Louis comes to Chantilly as the guest of Conde with the whole court behind him. Francois Vatel, the steward, has three days of banquets to serve and not enough roast for the tables on the first night. On the third morning the fish for the fast day has not arrived. He goes to his room, sets his sword against the door, and runs on it; the carts come through the gate while they are still looking for him. Madame de Sevigne writes the scene to her daughter within the week, and the letter outlives every guest at the table.
suggested_refs: The letters of Madame de Sevigne describing the death of Vatel at Chantilly, April 1671
sources: Madame de Sevigne, Letters, cited by the research pool without an edition or letter number

stops.name: Lobith: the crossing of the Rhine
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The army fords the Rhine at the Tolhuis below Lobith in a dry summer, against a Dutch guard of a few hundred horse. Fewer men are lost than at a bad hunt. Within weeks the medals are struck and the tapestries commissioned and the passage of the Rhine is being written as an epic. The Dutch cut their own dykes and drown their own country to stop him: they keep the province and lose the poem. The war Louis opens here to punish a republic of merchants runs six years and pulls in half of Europe.
suggested_refs: The Tolhuis crossing near Lobith, commemorated in French medals, tapestries and verse

stops.name: Maastricht: the first parallels, and the death of d'Artagnan
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unknown and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Louis brings his court to a siege. Vauban, given a free hand, digs the first full system of parallel trenches in the history of the art: three lines drawn concentric around the town, saps run forward between them, the garrison beaten by arithmetic instead of by assault. The place falls in thirteen days. Storming a half-moon before the Tongeren gate, d'Artagnan, who arrested Fouquet twelve years ago, is shot through the head. Far off on the Rhine, an army contractor named Samuel Oppenheimer is being recruited to feed the emperor against Louis.
suggested_refs: Vauban's parallel trenches at Maastricht, June 1673, the model for European siegecraft

stops.name: Valenciennes: the assault that went in at dawn
stops.date_confidence: the siege ran 28 February to 17 March 1677 with Louis present; month attested, day defaulted to 01. The research pool said the dawn assault was launched against Vauban's advice on timing, which verification reversed: the daylight attack was Vauban's own proposal, argued from surprise and coordination, and it was approved.
stops.campa: The rule of siegecraft is that a storm goes in at night. Vauban proposes the opposite at Valenciennes and is given it: the assault crosses at first light, when the defenders have stood down from the expected hour, and the covered way is carried with the town behind it. Louis is in the lines. The city is French inside a month and Cambrai falls in April. Everything the following year's peace confirms on this frontier is taken in the two winters when nobody expects an army to be out of quarters.
suggested_refs: The siege works of Valenciennes, 28 February to 17 March 1677

stops.name: Ghent: the winter stroke that ends the war
stops.date_confidence: month attested, day unknown and defaulted to 01
stops.campa: Louis takes Ghent in a rapid winter siege, with Ypres following, and the Dutch discover that six years of alliance have not moved the war off their own doorstep. They come to terms at Nijmegen in August. France keeps Franche-Comte, keeps the Flemish belt, and stands at the highest point the reign will reach: no coalition in the field, no rival capital that is not answering French letters in French. Louis is thirty-nine. Every war he fights after this one he fights against Europe assembled.
suggested_refs: The Treaty of Nijmegen, 1678, high-water mark of French power in Europe

stops.name: Marly: the house where invitation is the currency
stops.date_confidence: attested; work began 22 May 1679 and the chateau was complete by 1684. The research pool gave 1679-1686 and a coordinate about a kilometre off, 48.8697, 2.0897; both corrected here to Wikipedia's dates and 48.86389, 2.10000.
stops.campa: Twelve pavilions for the guests and one for the king, set in a valley behind Versailles, with water pumped up out of the Seine by a machine of fourteen wheels. Marly is small on purpose. No rank admits you here and no office does either: the king writes the list himself. Courtiers learn to use the name as a verb, asking Sire, Marly, in a corridor as he passes, and to read a whole season of favour out of the answer. The most expensive thing at Versailles turns out to be the way out of it.
stops.quote: Toutes les fois que je donne une place vacante, je fais cent mecontents et un ingrat.
stops.quote_source: attributed to Louis XIV by Voltaire, Le Siecle de Louis XIV (1751), ch. 26, seen here only through Wikiquote; Voltaire's text was not fetched
suggested_refs: The Machine de Marly on the Seine, which lifted water for the gardens of Marly and Versailles

stops.name: Strasbourg: a free city taken without a shot
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Louis has set up his own courts to rule which lands are dependencies of territories already ceded to him. They rule in his favour, and in peacetime thirty thousand troops surround a free imperial city. Strasbourg capitulates in a day. Louis enters on the twenty-third of October, and the cathedral organ is said to have played in his honour; the Lutheran cathedral is handed back to the Catholics the same week. No shot is fired and no war is declared. Europe reads the Reunions and begins counting, and the counting produces the Grand Alliance.
suggested_refs: The Chambers of Reunion and the annexation of Strasbourg, 23 October 1681

stops.name: Versailles: the government moves into a house
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The king, the household, the ministries, and some thousands of people whose only function is to be near him move to Versailles and stay. Jules Hardouin-Mansart is roofing the Hall of Mirrors over the terrace Le Vau left open, seventeen arched windows answered by seventeen arcades of glass, and it is finished within the year. Paris is twelve miles away and rules nothing. In August a grandson, Louis of Burgundy, is born in the palace. He will die in this building thirty-three years later, in the bedroom at the centre of it.
stops.quote_source: popularly attributed to Louis XIV and widely regarded by historians as apocryphal, first reported only in late 18th-century sources; included because it circulates, not because it is verified
suggested_refs: The Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, roofed by Hardouin-Mansart between 1678 and 1681

stops.name: Versailles: the queen has one happy day
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: An abscess forms under the queen's arm. The doctors bleed her and purge her and she dies at forty-four, twenty-three years married, with one surviving child out of six. Louis says of her that this is the first sorrow she ever caused him. She had learned French badly, played cards, ate chocolate and prayed, while the court watched her husband's mistresses ride in her own carriage for two decades. Her heart goes to the Val-de-Grace, the church his mother built in thanksgiving for his birth.
stops.quote: Since I have been Queen, I have had only one happy day.
stops.quote_source: reported last words of Maria Theresa of Spain, Versailles, 30 July 1683; a reported tradition, not documented at first hand
suggested_refs: The Val-de-Grace in Paris, built by Anne of Austria in thanksgiving for the birth of Louis XIV

stops.name: Versailles: the marriage nobody announces
stops.date_confidence: contested and left contested. Historians date the private ceremony either to 9 October 1683 or to January 1684; the research pool gives both and chooses neither. Dated here to the earlier, with the disagreement standing.
stops.campa: Three months after the queen's funeral, in a room at Versailles with the archbishop of Paris and a handful of witnesses, Louis marries Francoise d'Aubigne, Marquise de Maintenon, widow of the poet Scarron and former governess of his legitimised children. No announcement is made and none ever will be. She is not made queen and she is not crowned. For thirty-two years she is never away from him. She outlives him by four, at Saint-Cyr, in the school for poor noblewomen she founded, and dies there at eighty-three.
stops.quote: Je mettrais plutot toute l'Europe d'accord que deux femmes.
stops.quote_source: attributed to Louis XIV in the Comte de Mirabeau's Esprit de Mirabeau, vol. 1, seen here only through Wikiquote
suggested_refs: The Maison royale de Saint-Louis at Saint-Cyr, founded by Madame de Maintenon and her retirement after 1715

stops.name: Fontainebleau: the Edict of Nantes revoked
stops.date_confidence: attested at 18 October by the geography lens; the chronology lens gives the year only. The Code Noir, also 1685, is carried in this campa because the research pool gives it no month and no place beyond 'France'.
stops.campa: The Edict of Nantes has stood for eighty-seven years, granting the Protestants of France worship, courts and fortified towns. Louis revokes it at Fontainebleau. Temples come down, ministers are given fifteen days to leave the kingdom and the laity are forbidden to go; between two and three hundred thousand Huguenots go anyway. The same year he signs the Code Noir, which fixes the legal condition of the enslaved in the colonies and the schedule of their punishments. In 1787 Louis XVI will restore the Protestants a civil status, and the text will name what his ancestor did in this house.
stops.quote: Louis, by the grace of God king of France and Navarre, to all present and to come, greeting: ... we have determined that we can do nothing better ... than entirely to revoke the said Edict of Nantes
stops.quote_source: Edict of Fontainebleau, October 1685, English translation, Fordham University Internet Modern History Sourcebook, fetched directly
suggested_refs: The Edict of Fontainebleau, October 1685, and the Code Noir of the same year
sources: Fordham University, Internet Modern History Sourcebook

stops.name: Versailles gardens: the king recarved into a Roman suicide
stops.date_confidence: the recarving is dated 1687; month and day defaulted to 01. The statue was moved about the gardens for some sixteen years before reaching the site near the Lake of the Swiss Guards.
stops.campa: Bernini's marble of the king on a rearing horse arrives from Rome in 1685, and Louis hates it: too much motion, and a face he takes as an insult. He orders it destroyed. Girardon talks him out of that and recarves it instead, cutting a new head, adding a crested helmet and flames at the horse's feet, turning the living king into Marcus Curtius riding into the chasm to save Rome. The statue is walked around the gardens for sixteen years and set at last by the Lake of the Swiss Guards, at the far end, facing away.
suggested_refs: Girardon's recarving of Bernini's Louis XIV as Marcus Curtius, near the Lake of the Swiss Guards at Versailles

segments.name: The Rhine Burns, the Succession Fails

stops.name: Heidelberg: the Palatinate made a desert
stops.date_confidence: the devastation is dated 1689, with a second burning in 1693; month and day defaulted to 01. This whole war is absent from the chronology, geography and afterlife research and reaches the atlas only through the corpus. Pin inherited from joseph_oppenheimer.journey.json, which places the Heidelberg Judengasse at 49.4094, 8.6946; the interlock lens reported 49.3988, 8.6724, a value that appears in no journey file.
stops.campa: Louvois orders the Palatinate burned so that no imperial army can be fed in it. Heidelberg, Mannheim, Worms and Speyer go up, the castle is mined, the vines are cut. The Nine Years' War runs nine years and empties the treasury Colbert filled. On the Rhine, Samuel Oppenheimer victuals the emperor's armies against Louis and has his son Emanuel seized as a hostage against faster delivery to Philippsburg. Nine years after the fires, in the Judengasse of the burned town, a boy is born who will be called Joseph Suss Oppenheimer.
suggested_refs: The ruined castle of Heidelberg, mined on French orders during the Nine Years' War

stops.name: Compiegne: sixty thousand men besiege a fort built for the purpose
stops.date_confidence: the research pool gives the year only, with no month or day; defaulted to 01. The camp of Compiegne is conventionally placed in September 1698.
stops.campa: An army is camped at Compiegne to besiege a fortification put up for it to take, watched by the ambassadors of every power that has just made peace with France. The court comes out to see it and the ladies are given seats on the ramparts. The following year Girardon's bronze of the king on horseback goes up in the middle of the Place Vendome, reputed the first large equestrian statue cast in a single piece since antiquity. In 1700 a Bourbon takes the throne of Spain, and the peace lasts three years.
stops.quote: Il n'y a plus de Pyrenees.
stops.quote_source: attributed to Louis XIV on the accession of his grandson to the Spanish throne in 1700; reported in Voltaire, Le Siecle de Louis XIV (1751), ch. 28, seen here through Wikiquote and not traced to a primary document
suggested_refs: The camp of Compiegne, 1698, staged for the ambassadors of the powers that signed at Ryswick
sources: standard biographies cited by the research pool without an edition

stops.name: Versailles: the chapel finished, and nothing after it
stops.date_confidence: completion dated 1710 in the research pool, after eleven years' work; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: After eleven years the palace chapel is done, the fifth on the site and the first meant to last: a nave of white stone under a painted vault, the king's tribune at the upper level, the court below him and the altar in front of them. He hears mass here every morning. The court, standing beneath, faces the tribune rather than the altar, and the arrangement is not remarked on because it has stopped being visible. It is the last great building of the reign. The wars have taken whatever would have paid for another.
suggested_refs: The royal chapel at Versailles, completed 1710, the last major work of the reign

stops.name: Marly: the heir dies six days after his wife
stops.date_confidence: attested. The Grand Dauphin's death at Meudon on 14 April 1711 is carried in this campa because Meudon has no coordinate in the research pool.
stops.campa: The Grand Dauphin died of smallpox at Meudon in April 1711, forty-nine years old, having been heir for half a century. Ten months later measles goes through the family at Marly. Marie-Adelaide of Savoy, married to the Duke of Burgundy at Versailles at fifteen, dies on the twelfth of February; her husband, who nursed her and would not leave the room, dies on the eighteenth. What is left of the direct line is a boy of two, and he will reign fifty-nine years as Louis XV.
suggested_refs: The Chateau de Marly, where the Duke of Burgundy and his wife died within six days in February 1712

stops.name: Versailles: the two crowns forbidden to meet
stops.date_confidence: attested for the main Utrecht treaties. The stop is pinned at Versailles, where Louis was; Utrecht has no coordinate in the research pool.
stops.campa: Thirteen years of war over the Spanish inheritance end at Utrecht. Louis's grandson keeps Madrid and renounces France in writing, in July 1712, before the negotiators will proceed at all, and the treaties of April 1713 write into the law of Europe that the two crowns must never rest on one head. This is the clause Mazarin bought on the Bidasoa in 1659 and Louis spent his reign trying to make void. France keeps its frontiers and loses everything else it went to war for.
suggested_refs: The renunciation of Philip V, 10 July 1712, and the Utrecht treaties of 11 April 1713

stops.name: Versailles: the death of the king
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Gangrene takes the left leg in August. He refuses amputation, settles his papers, and takes leave of the court and of his great-grandson of five. He dies on the first of September, four days short of seventy-seven, in the seventy-third year of a reign that began when he was four. No one now alive at Versailles can remember another king. The funeral procession to Saint-Denis is jeered along the road, and the taverns on the route do business as it passes.
stops.quote: Je m'en vais, mais l'Etat demeurera toujours.
stops.quote_source: attributed to Louis XIV on his deathbed by the Marquis de Dangeau, Memoire sur la mort de Louis XIV; reached here through Wikiquote and not traced to Dangeau's text
suggested_refs: The king's bedchamber at Versailles, where Louis XIV died on 1 September 1715
sources: Wikipedia, 'Timeline of Louis XIV of France'

stops.name: Saint-Denis: laid among the kings
stops.date_confidence: attested. Pin inherited from saint_denis.journey.json, which uses 48.9355, 2.3597; the research pool gave 48.9354 with two different longitudes.
stops.campa: He is put into the crypt at Saint-Denis, in the abbey raised over the grave of Saint Denis, beheaded on Montmartre and buried in a stranger's field, among Bourbons and Valois and the Merovingian kings whose oil was poured on him at Reims. His heart goes separately to the Jesuit church of Saint-Louis in Paris, by the custom of the house. Sixty years from now his great-great-great-grandson Louis XVI will be consecrated at Reims with the same phial, and will not be brought here at all when the time comes.
suggested_refs: The Bourbon vault in the crypt of the Basilica of Saint-Denis

stops.name: Place Vendome, Paris: the bronze horse goes to the furnace
stops.date_confidence: the statue was erected in 1699 and destroyed in 1792 or 1793; the research pool gives the range without a precise date. Dated here to 1792, month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: The bronze king rides in the middle of his own square for ninety-three years. The Revolution pulls him down and sends him to the furnaces, where the metal of an equestrian statue is worth more as cannon than as a king. Girardon had cast him in a single pour, the first to manage it since antiquity, and it takes rather less skill to unmake. A reduced version survives and is carried into the Louvre, the palace Louis left for Versailles a hundred and twenty years before.
suggested_refs: The small surviving version of Girardon's Place Vendome equestrian statue, Musee du Louvre

stops.name: Saint-Denis: the trench and the lime
stops.date_confidence: the Convention's order and the two waves of exhumation fall in August and October 1793; day defaulted to 01. The account in the research pool does not name Louis XIV specifically among the disturbed remains, though he was interred here, and the campa does not claim his body was identified.
stops.campa: The Convention orders the royal tombs opened. In August and again in October the coffins come out of the crypt, the bodies go into two trenches in the ground north of the church, and quicklime is shovelled in on top of them. When the church reopens under Napoleon in 1806 the kings are still in the trenches. A Bourbon commission digging in 1817 finds three bodies with any shape left; the rest, fragments of some hundred and fifty-eight people, go into a single ossuary with the names cut in marble above them, unsortable.
suggested_refs: The common ossuary of the Bourbon and Valois remains in the crypt of Saint-Denis, assembled after 1817

stops.name: Place des Victoires, Paris: a Bourbon put back on the horse
stops.date_confidence: the Bosio statue is dated 1828; month and day defaulted to 01. The demolition of the Desjardins statue is dated 1792, the wooden pyramid 1793 and the Desaix 1810.
stops.campa: Desjardins had shown him in gilt bronze, crowned by Victory, treading Cerberus. It comes down in 1792. A wooden pyramid stands on the pedestal in 1793 and a nude General Desaix in 1810, and that is taken away in turn. In 1828 Charles X, the last Bourbon to try the throne, puts an ancestor back on the spot: Bosio's Louis in Roman dress on a rearing horse, twelve metres high, copied from the Bronze Horseman at Saint Petersburg, with an iron fence around him.
suggested_refs: Bosio's equestrian Louis XIV of 1828 at the Place des Victoires, third statue on the site

stops.name: Versailles: the palace made into a museum of the nation
stops.date_confidence: attested; the museum was begun in 1833 and inaugurated 30 June 1837
stops.campa: The royal family left in October 1789, the Convention stripped the pictures for the Louvre in 1792, and the furniture was auctioned over the following year; by 1793 anyone could walk through the state apartments, and an art school was working in some of the empty rooms. Franz Mesmer takes lodgings in 1801 in the emptied town beside the emptied palace. Louis-Philippe, a king made by a chamber of deputies, spends his own money turning the Sun King's house into a Museum of the History of France and opens it in June 1837.
suggested_refs: The Galerie des Batailles at Versailles, centrepiece of Louis-Philippe's Museum of the History of France

stops.name: Nuneham House: the geologist and the heart
stops.date_confidence: traditional and disputed. The dinner is dated 1848 in some tellings; the story is first printed by Nathaniel Hawthorne in 1863 and repeated by Augustus Hare in 1900, and its veracity is questioned. Month and day defaulted to 01. The coordinate is a village-level approximation carried from the research pool.
stops.campa: The embalmed heart taken from the body at Versailles passes, by way of the Revolution and a dealer, into an English collection, and is kept at Nuneham in a case. The geologist William Buckland, who made a practice of eating his way through the animal kingdom, is shown it after dinner. He is said to have declared that he had eaten many strange things but never the heart of a king, and then to have eaten it. Nathaniel Hawthorne prints the story in 1863 and Augustus Hare repeats it in 1900, and nobody who was at that table ever wrote it down.
suggested_refs: Nuneham House, Oxfordshire, and the reliquary heart of the disputed Buckland anecdote
sources: Wikipedia, 'William Buckland', citing Nathaniel Hawthorne, Our Old Home (1863) and Augustus Hare, The Story of My Life (1900)

stops.name: Versailles: the mirrors made again
stops.date_confidence: the Grand Versailles campaign began in 2003 and the Hall of Mirrors restoration was completed in 2006; month and day defaulted to 01
stops.campa: John D. Rockefeller Jr. gives roughly two million dollars between 1925 and 1928 to keep the roofs on. The Royal Opera reopens in 1957, UNESCO inscribes the palace and its eight hundred hectares of park in 1979, and the cyclone of December 1999 takes down enough of the park that the gardens are replanted to Le Notre's plan. The Hall of Mirrors is finished again in 2006. Marcel Proust spent five months in 1905 at a hotel a few hundred metres from these gates and never once walked over to look at it.
suggested_refs: The Hall of Mirrors at Versailles after the Grand Versailles restoration of 2003 to 2006
